contexts.text:
Community activity notice

Fictional practice notice. The Green Lane Centre is holding an activity morning on Saturday. A talk at ten introduces vocabulary used on food labels, followed by a relaxed group walk at eleven. Registration is free, but places for the label-reading workshop must be booked because the room is small. Visitors should bring their own water bottle. The notice gives times and arrangements; it does not promise a cure or prescribe a personal diet or exercise programme.

A manageable research question

Fictional practice account. A postgraduate student wanted to investigate every aspect of language learning in one dissertation. Her tutor asked her to narrow the scope. She decided to compare the vocabulary records kept by twelve volunteers in one class over six weeks. The library supplied background literature, and the study needed no expensive equipment. Her findings would describe that small group. She planned to explain its limits rather than claim that twelve people represented every language learner.

Two ways of sharing instructions

Fictional practice passage. A language club tested two versions of a welcome guide. One version listed rules in short paragraphs; the other added a diagram of the room and examples of common questions. Eighteen new members read a guide and answered the same questions. The group recorded their answers but did not record their ages. Most readers of the illustrated version found the room more easily. The organisers called this a small trial and proposed testing the guide again before making broader claims.

Two imagined places to stay

Fictional practice listings. Valley Cottage has two bedrooms and a small kitchen. It stands in a quiet rural village, twenty minutes from the station by local bus. Guests bring their own food. Harbour Rooms offers compact rooms above a busy coastal café. Breakfast is included, and the ferry terminal is a five-minute walk away. Neither listing gives a price. A traveller choosing between them should compare the stated facilities and location rather than assume that a picturesque view guarantees a luxurious stay.

A strip of habitat

Fictional practice account. A nature club asked a grounds team to leave a narrow strip of vegetation uncut beside a field. Members recorded insects and birds from the path without handling them. They noted different kinds of flora and fauna, but did not try to estimate the population across the whole region. The final report described the observations and recommended continuing the records through another season. Its claim concerned one small habitat, not proof that every species in the region was increasing.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

Four speakers describe different sources of support and shared interests. Speaker A watches films with classmates. Speaker B turns to an approachable university tutor for study advice because communication with the parents is difficult. Speaker C plans to ask an older brother for help buying a car. Speaker D shares an interest in classical music with a grandfather who plays the cello.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The student describes a small immediate family within a much larger extended family, including twenty-five cousins. Family gatherings are lively, and the family is close-knit. Both parents took an active part in childhood life and helped settle disagreements fairly. The student is said to resemble the maternal grandmother physically, while sharing the father’s stubborn temperament and ability in mathematics.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

Sallyanne Cullen enrols her daughter Alexandra, called Alex, at Ascot Child-Care Centre. Alex has just turned three and belongs in the toddler group. Her birthday is 8 November. Her brother Fraser is five. The address is 108 Park Road, Maidstone, and the contact number 34678890 belongs to Alex’s grandmother. Alex gets on with other children, does not sleep easily during the day and can dress herself. Care is needed on Monday and Tuesday; the grandmother covers Wednesday. The requested collection time is four o’clock.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The supplied lecture organises examples of early development into social, physical, communication and cognitive skills. It moves from infancy to the toddler stage and then middle childhood. Examples include gestures, imitation, taking turns, imaginative play, sorting objects and later sequencing and ordering. The speaker notes that children develop at different rates. These are examples in a language-learning recording, not an individual developmental assessment.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The student recalls a happy childhood and enjoys reminiscing with the sisters. Hot summer weather brings back memories of childhood holidays. The student contrasts a formerly strong ability to memorise dates with greater difficulty remembering things now. Current strategies include visualising an association and writing reminder notes.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

This supplied language lesson discusses the heart, blood flow and arteries, introducing words for body processes and health problems. Its sequence connects blocked arteries with problems affecting the heart or brain. The purpose here is to recognise the recording’s vocabulary and sequence; the recording is not a source of personal diagnosis or treatment instructions.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The second supplied health-language passage turns to exercise vocabulary. It describes aerobic activity, breathing, heart rate and calories, and names activities including walking, jogging, swimming and cycling. It also explicitly says that a doctor may recommend a different amount or pace for an individual. This is recording comprehension, not a personalised exercise plan.
bath, bathe, birth, breath, breathe, death, growth, health, mouth (verb), mouth (noun), teeth, teethe, writhe

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The six practice sentences contain breath, teething and teeth, health, birth, writhing and breathe. They illustrate the distinction between nouns and verbs and the sounds in related forms. References to pain or difficulty breathing are supplied language scenes, not new treatment advice.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The first speaker accepts that working hard and experiencing ups and downs are part of life. The second enjoys extreme sports and describes living on the edge. The third expects plans to be spoiled and expresses a pessimistic attitude. The fourth takes a positive outlook and wants to live life to the full. These are the speakers’ views rather than rules about the right way to live.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

Julie Roberts discusses school-holiday activities. She suggests using the first days to organise supplies, booking popular day trips online and visiting libraries for changing activities. The website ideas include a reusable craft kit, a household-material lava lamp, a prepared treasure hunt, filming original stories, non-cooking kitchen activities, sport for older children and gardening projects. The treasure hunt needs preparation; story time needs a digital camera; kitchen time can be messy; gardening may need help from someone with building skills. This is the broadcast’s activity account, not a safety guide.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The student began kindergarten at four and initially did not enjoy it. Primary school was better, and the mother taught the student in the junior school. A scholarship made a private high school affordable. The student attended a single-sex school and personally felt this helped concentration. That final judgement is an opinion in the recording.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The talk concerns choosing a postgraduate research topic. It recommends knowing the existing literature, developing broad knowledge of the specialism, identifying relevant questions and defining the scope. A controversy or theory may provide a focus. Financial resources matter, and external agencies or local industry might offer funding. The tutor can help check the work and findings.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

A French teacher recalls struggling with vocabulary, then becoming good at written tests, essays, translation and grammar. Living in France exposed a different difficulty: everyday conversation. Ordering coffee and making telephone enquiries about accommodation were hard because people spoke quickly. The account argues for practising functional communication alongside accuracy.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The student argues for conversation with native speakers and sometimes putting textbooks aside. A good teacher, in the student’s view, can explain clearly and understands learning another language. The student identifies pronunciation and unfamiliar individual sounds as difficulties for people learning the first language. These are attributed learning opinions.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The first speaker lives in a peaceful village with a busy Sunday market. The second describes a coastal place with beaches and water sports, currently reached by ferry. The third describes a cosmopolitan city with many shopping malls, reliable public transport and some air pollution. The fourth lives above a valley in a picturesque mountain village, often reached by train because the roads are steep and winding.

The first speaker gets engrossed in work and loses track of time. The second can spend too long plaiting thick hair and once almost missed a wedding ceremony. The third dislikes lateness, sets clocks and watches ten minutes fast and carries a spare watch. The examples contrast losing time, time-consuming preparation and deliberate punctuality.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The supplied historical lecture traces dentistry from ancient evidence and written explanations to later specialised practice. It mentions early drilled teeth in the Indus Valley, the historical tooth-worm belief, Egyptian written records and chewing sticks used before modern toothbrushes. It contrasts different access to dental treatment in medieval Europe and describes Pierre Fauchard’s naval experience and influential book. Historical remedies mentioned in the source are not recommendations for use.

The recording describes meerkats on the semi-arid plains of southern Africa. They avoid dense vegetation and use burrows dug with strong forelegs, or crevices between rocks when digging is not possible. Their food includes insects, spiders and snails, with occasional other prey or roots. A keen sense of smell helps them forage.

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

The supplied lesson compares Venus, Mercury and Saturn while discussing possible human settlement. Venus is linked with thick clouds and surface craters; Mercury with proximity to the Sun and little atmosphere; Saturn with rings and the Voyager probe. Treat the passage as the supplied edition’s simplified listening account, rather than a current scientific reference or a claim that every description is complete.
astronaut, atmosphere, commercial, explorer, exploration, galaxy, horizon, horizontal, outer, satellite, solar system, sustain, universal

Listening review: independently written notes checked against the supplied script. These are not a word-for-word transcript.

John and Susan discuss space exploration after John returns from a conference. Susan questions the expenditure and initially favours robots. John points to knowledge gained and the limits of pre-programmed machines. The conversation values proven equipment and identifies communication delays as a deep-space concern. John argues that ambitious projects can begin before all technology is ready, proposing protected underground settlement; Susan remains doubtful. Both consider boredom, lack of open nature and managing essential supplies. Their predictions and proposals are opinions in the source dialogue.
